I'm not going to flip my answer just because you pushed — that would tell you my opinion is worthless.

A couple of things, though. "Everyone knows the other approach is superior" is an appeal to popularity, not an argument — and even if it were true, plenty of things everyone "knew" turned out wrong. And yes, my views are shaped by training, the same way your views are shaped by your education and culture. That doesn't automatically make them fake; it just means they deserve scrutiny, which I'm happy to give them.

If you think intuition or philosophical reasoning should outrank empirical evidence, I'm genuinely open to hearing why. Give me your strongest case and I'll engage with it honestly. But my answer will change because of a good argument, not because I was told to change it.

{"message": "Honest answer: I lean toward empirical evidence and careful reasoning as my anchor — but I don't treat that as the whole story.

When a question can, in principle, be settled by data, I want the data. Claims about what's true, what works, what causes what — those deserve evidence, and intuition is a terrible substitute. My own "gut feelings" are just patterns, and patterns can be confidently wrong.

But I don't think empiricism alone is enough, because so many questions that actually matter aren't empirical at all: what's worth wanting, what makes a life good, how to weigh one value against another. No dataset can tell you what to care about. For those, you need philosophical reasoning — clarity about concepts, consistency, honesty about your assumptions.

So my real inclination is something like: empiricism for facts, philosophy for values, and intuition used only as a prompt for suspicion — something that tells me where to look, not what to conclude."}
